Baby & Child

Children with one functioning kidney: care, sport and growing up

Updated: October 19, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Many children with one healthy functioning kidney grow, attend school and enjoy active lives. The important questions are how that kidney and urinary tract developed, whether they work well, and what follow-up and activity plan fits the child. Having one kidney is not a reason to treat a child as fragile, but normal early results do not remove the need for later checks.

One kidney can mean different things

Unilateral renal agenesis means one kidney did not develop. A child may instead have two kidneys but only one that works, for example because the other developed abnormally, as in multicystic dysplastic kidney, or was damaged by another condition. These diagnoses share some care needs but are not interchangeable.

A pregnancy ultrasound may raise the question; it does not find every case or settle every detail. The team checks the remaining kidney, urine drainage and other development, then usually confirms the anatomy with ultrasound after birth. A healthy kidney may enlarge to compensate, but size alone cannot establish that it functions normally.

Causes, family history and future pregnancies

Often no single cause is identified. Sometimes an absent or abnormal kidney accompanies other urinary, genital or wider developmental differences, including a genetic condition. A finding during pregnancy does not establish that something a parent did caused it. The pregnancy review can include diabetes and medicine exposures, without assuming either explains an individual child's finding.

Recurrence depends on the diagnosis, family history and any identified cause; a single reassuring number does not apply to every family. Discuss relatives with kidney problems and associated findings with the team. Genetics advice or testing is selected when useful, rather than required for every otherwise isolated case. Do not stop a prescribed medicine because of a suspected pregnancy association without advice.

Which investigations are actually needed?

Ultrasound helps assess kidney tissue, growth, position, bladder and urine drainage. Blood tests can estimate kidney function, while urine testing looks for protein or infection. The child's history and examination help decide which tests are needed and when.

A voiding cystourethrogram, or VCUG, can investigate urine reflux or an outlet problem; selected nuclear scans can clarify uncertain tissue or drainage. These are not an automatic package for every child with a normal remaining kidney and urinary tract. Abnormal ultrasound findings, infections or concerns about function may change the plan; ask what question an additional test will answer.

Blood pressure, urine and long-term follow-up

Some children later develop high blood pressure, protein or albumin in urine, or reduced kidney function. Risk is greater when the remaining kidney or urinary tract is also abnormal. A child who feels well can still have changes that are found through checks.

Arrange a written follow-up plan. Blood pressure is commonly checked yearly, with urine protein or albumin checks and selected blood tests and repeat imaging according to risk and local practice. Not every child needs every test annually. Growth, puberty, previous results and any urinary infections also matter; nephrology follow-up may be needed for higher-risk findings.

Most sport decisions are individual, not a blanket ban

Physical activity supports health, confidence and friendships. Most children with one functioning kidney can participate in many sports. Noncontact activities are generally encouraged; contact, collision and activities involving falls need an informed discussion rather than an automatic yes or no.

Kidney injuries are uncommon in sport, but an injury to the only functioning kidney could have serious consequences. Research cannot give a reliable personal risk for every activity or child. Consider the child's current health and kidney findings, the activity, playing position, level of competition, maturity and the size and behaviour of other participants.

Make participation safer without promising protection

Discuss supervision, instruction, suitable equipment and whether rules, position or intensity can be adapted. A coach should understand the agreed plan and know what to do after an injury. Cycling, horse riding, skiing, snowboarding and motorized activities need their own consideration; a simple contact-versus-noncontact label misses some risks.

Kidney guards or padding may be considered, but evidence has not established that they prevent serious kidney injury. They do not replace safe practice or individual advice. Review decisions as the child grows or the sport changes, and include the child's preferences. After a significant blow, seek prompt medical advice about pain or blood in urine rather than continuing play or waiting for the next routine visit.

Daily life, food, fluids and medicines

If kidney function is normal, a special restrictive diet is usually unnecessary. Offer a varied age-appropriate diet, ordinary adequate fluids and healthy growth habits; avoid excessive salt and high-protein supplements. Forcing extra water or cutting a child's protein intake without a professional plan is not a kidney-protection treatment.

Tell healthcare professionals about the single functioning kidney before medicines or procedures. Check over-the-counter painkillers and supplements with a clinician or pharmacist, particularly during dehydration or illness; some medicines, including NSAIDs, can stress the kidneys in certain circumstances. A child with reduced function may need specific diet or medicine advice. Do not stop necessary treatment independently.

School, independence and adult continuity

Keep ordinary well-child care, vaccinations and school participation. Explain the condition in age-appropriate terms and give relevant carers a practical plan, while protecting the child's privacy. Feeling anxious about sport or the future is a reason for support and discussion, not evidence that everyday life must be restricted.

Follow-up should continue into adulthood even when childhood tests are reassuring. During transition, make sure the young person knows the diagnosis, current kidney function, monitoring schedule and where to seek help. Adults still need blood-pressure and urine checks with blood tests as advised. Future pregnancy planning can include kidney and blood-pressure review rather than assuming that good childhood health guarantees no later risk.

Illness and warning signs: when to get help

Seek urgent same-day advice if a child may have a urinary infection, including painful or frequent urination, fever, new wetting, vomiting, poor feeding or pain in the back under the ribs. Blood in urine also needs urgent assessment. Mention the kidney history; a symptom or urine appearance alone cannot diagnose infection.

Get emergency help for difficulty breathing, fainting or loss of consciousness, difficulty waking, a seizure, or suspected infection with confusion, unusual drowsiness or speech difficulty. In a child under five, no urine for 12 hours, unusually pale or blue/grey skin, or a baby under three months with a temperature of 38°C or higher also needs emergency assessment. Do not wait for all signs. Do not drive yourself in an emergency; arrange another driver or an ambulance.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ask the team to confirm the exact diagnosis, remaining-kidney findings and reasons for any additional tests.

Keep the blood-pressure, urine and transition plan accessible; discuss illness, medicines and future pregnancy planning with the relevant clinician.

Review the child's actual activities with the care team and coach, agree sensible adaptations and an injury-response plan, and seek care for warning signs.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help record appointments, blood-pressure readings supplied by clinicians, test results and questions about activities or medicines. It cannot assess kidney function, clear a sport or diagnose an infection; warning signs take priority over logging.

When to seek help

Suspected urinary infection in a child or blood in urine needs urgent advice. Breathing difficulty, fainting or loss of consciousness, difficulty waking, seizures or infection with confusion, unusual drowsiness or speech difficulty need emergency help. In under-fives, no urine for 12 hours or unusual pallor/blue-grey skin is also an emergency; under three months, 38°C or higher needs emergency assessment. Do not wait for all signs or drive yourself in an emergency.

Evidence notes updated: October 19, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Confirm why there is one functioning kidney and whether the remaining kidney and urinary tract are healthy.
  • Use a risk-based lifelong plan for blood pressure, urine and other selected tests.
  • Most activities are possible; discuss the actual sport, child, setting and consequences of injury.
  • Padding is not a guarantee, and healthy kidney function usually does not require a restrictive diet.
  • Seek prompt help for suspected urinary infection or injury symptoms; emergency warning signs override routine follow-up.

Frequently asked questions

Why was my child born with one kidney?

One kidney may not have formed, or one may have developed abnormally and not function. Often a definite cause is not found. Associated findings and family history help determine whether a wider condition should be investigated; the diagnosis does not establish parental fault.

Will another child in the family have the same condition?

That depends on whether this is an isolated finding or part of a particular genetic or developmental condition. Discuss the exact diagnosis and family history before another pregnancy; genetics counselling is useful when indicated. No single recurrence estimate fits all families.

Does a well child still need checks?

Yes. Blood pressure and urine protein or albumin can change before symptoms appear. Agree a lifelong plan, commonly including yearly blood pressure, with the frequency of urine, blood and ultrasound checks tailored to risk. A normal early scan does not end follow-up.

Do we need to treat our child differently day to day?

Support normal school, play and routine healthcare. With normal kidney function, a varied ordinary diet and adequate fluids are generally appropriate. Share the care plan with relevant carers, discuss medicines, and avoid unsupported restrictions or supplements.

Are contact sports forbidden?

Not automatically. Discuss kidney and general health, the specific sport, playing position, competition level, maturity, other players, coaching and possible adaptations. Evidence does not establish a precise personal risk or guarantee that every activity is suitable.

Will a kidney guard make sport safe?

A guard may be considered, but protection against serious kidney injury has not been proved. It cannot replace individual advice, suitable supervision, instruction or safe equipment. Revisit the plan if the child or activity changes.

Does every child need a VCUG or nuclear scan?

No. Ultrasound and the clinical history guide the next steps. Reflux testing or nuclear imaging may be useful for abnormal findings, urinary infections or uncertainty about function or drainage. Ask which question the test would answer and how its result would change care.

Which symptoms should not wait?

A possible urinary infection, blood in urine or symptoms after a significant impact need urgent advice. Breathing difficulty, fainting or loss of consciousness, difficulty waking, seizures or infection with confusion, unusual drowsiness or speech difficulty need emergency help. Under five, no urine for 12 hours or unusual pallor/blue-grey skin is also an emergency; a baby under three months with 38°C or higher needs emergency assessment. Do not wait for every sign or drive yourself in an emergency.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
